abstract: Nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD) limits the abundance of transcripts containing premature termination codons (PTCs) and regulates other endogenous mRNAs. How distinct transcripts respond to reduced NMD capacity in liver disease remains poorly understood. Here, we found that hepatic UPF1 and UPF2 protein abundance was markedly reduced in human alcohol-associated hepatitis. Hepatocyte-specific Upf2 deletion in mice caused liver injury, cell death, and macrophage accumulation, with innate immune gene induction evident by day 11. Integrated intron-exon RNA-seq analysis identified 259 protein-coding candidate NMD-regulated genes, including genes involved in inflammation, stress responses, and metabolism. Canonical NMD substrates, including the PTC-containing isoforms of Tra2b, Hnrnpl, and Ptbp2, accumulated markedly following hepatocyte-specific Upf2 deletion. In contrast, partial Upf2 knockdown in primary mouse hepatocytes induced NMD-targeted inflammatory genes, including Ccl2, Ccl7, Icam1, and Ifit2 while producing only modest changes in the examined PTC-containing isoforms. Human alcohol-associated hepatitis livers likewise exhibited increased CCL2, ICAM1, and IFIT2 expression, accompanied by modest and variable changes in these canonical NMD substrates. These findings support differential transcript responsiveness to reduced NMD capacity and indicate that selected PTC-containing substrates may incompletely reflect its effects on endogenous gene regulation. Together, our results identify hepatocyte NMD as a restraint on inflammatory gene expression and suggest that its suppression may contribute to hepatic inflammation in alcohol-associated hepatitis.
